clinicalScope: Anatomical and clinical overview of the human heart for adult patients in low‑resource East African hospitals
subject: Anatomy
summary: The heart is a four‑chambered muscular pump that sits in the middle mediastinum and drives blood circulation. This page explains its development, structure, relations and how anatomy guides bedside assessment and common low‑resource investigations.

sections.p: The heart is a cone‑shaped organ composed of two atria and two ventricles that functions as the central circulatory pump.
b: Four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.
Three wall layers: epicardium (visceral pericardium), myocardium (contractile muscle), endocardium (inner lining).
Two valve systems: atrioventricular (tricuspid, mitral) and semilunar (pulmonary, aortic).
Located in the middle mediastinum, between the lungs, with the apex pointing to the left 5th intercostal space.

sections.p: The heart forms from the mesodermal cardiogenic plate and undergoes looping, septation and valve formation between weeks 3‑8 of gestation.
b: Cardiac tube elongates and folds (D‑loop) establishing left‑right orientation.
Atrial and ventricular septa develop from endocardial cushions and muscular growth.
Failure of septation leads to congenital defects such as atrial septal defect (ASD).
Key signalling pathways: NKX2‑5, TBX5, NOTCH.

sections.p: Understanding surface landmarks and neighbouring structures aids physical examination and imaging interpretation.
b: Anterior (sternocostal) surface: right ventricle dominates; left ventricle forms left border.
Inferior (diaphragmatic) surface: left ventricle forms most of the surface; right ventricle wraps around.
Base faces posteriorly toward the left atrium and the pulmonary veins.
Relations: esophagus posterior, lungs laterally, diaphragm inferiorly, great vessels superiorly.

sections.p: Coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses and deliver oxygenated blood to the myocardium.
b: Right coronary artery (RCA) supplies right atrium, right ventricle, SA node (≈60%) and AV node (≈80%).
Left coronary artery (LCA) bifurcates into left anterior descending (LAD) and circumflex (LCx).
LAD supplies anterior septum and apex; LCx supplies lateral left ventricle and left atrium.
Coronary venous drainage follows the cardiac veins into the coronary sinus.

sections.p: Autonomic innervation modulates heart rate and contractility; lymphatics maintain interstitial fluid balance.
b: Sympathetic fibers (cervical & thoracic ganglia) increase rate and force via β1‑adrenergic receptors.
Parasympathetic (vagus nerve) slows rate via muscarinic receptors.
Cardiac plexus lies anterior to the aortic arch; fibers converge on the sino‑atrial (SA) and atrio‑ventricular (AV) nodes.
Lymphatics follow coronary arteries to the tracheobronchial nodes.

sections.p: Microscopic layers explain functional properties and disease susceptibility.
b: Epicardium: mesothelial cells over connective tissue; site of coronary artery origin.
Myocardium: striated cardiac muscle with intercalated discs (desmosomes, gap junctions).
Endocardium: simple squamous endothelium over a thin subendothelial layer.
Valvular tissue: dense collagenous core covered by endothelium.

sections.p: The heart’s pump action follows a precise sequence of electrical and mechanical events.
b: Systole: ventricular contraction ejects blood into pulmonary artery and aorta.
Diastole: relaxation allows ventricular filling; atrial contraction contributes ~15% of ventricular volume.
Stroke volume = end‑diastolic volume – end‑systolic volume; cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
Frank‑Starling law: increased preload stretches myocardium, enhancing contractility.

sections.p: Anatomical knowledge directs bedside maneuvers, procedural safety and interpretation of common investigations.
b: Apex beat palpated at the 5th left intercostal space, mid‑clavicular line – guides assessment of left ventricular size.
Carotid pulse assessment reflects left ventricular output; diminished pulse may suggest LV failure.
Pericardial tamponade signs (Beck’s triad) arise from fluid compressing the low‑pressure right chambers.
Coronary artery dominance (RCA vs LCA) influences infarct patterns and surgical planning.

sections.p: Trauma and disease often target specific anatomic zones.
b: Blunt chest trauma can cause myocardial contusion, most often in the right ventricle (anterior location).
Rheumatic heart disease frequently damages the mitral valve leaflets, leading to stenosis or regurgitation.
Ischemic injury follows coronary distribution; LAD occlusion produces anterior wall MI.
Pericardial effusion accumulates in the pericardial cavity, limiting diastolic filling.

sections.p: Physical exam and low‑resource imaging complement each other in diagnosing cardiac conditions.
b: Auscultation: S1 (closure of AV valves) and S2 (closure of semilunar valves); murmurs localise valve lesions.
Palpation: displaced apex suggests cardiomegaly; a thrill indicates turbulent flow.
Chest X‑ray (available in most district hospitals): assesses cardiac silhouette, pulmonary congestion, and aortic arch width.
Echocardiography (if available): evaluates chamber size, wall motion, valve morphology, and pericardial fluid.

t.b: What is the cardiac silhouette size? – Cardiomegaly if cardiothoracic ratio >0.5 on PA film; suggests chronic volume overload.
Is there evidence of ischemia or chamber enlargement? – ST‑segment changes indicate acute MI; QRS axis shift suggests ventricular hypertrophy.

sections.p: Anatomical variants influence clinical decision‑making, especially in surgery and interventional cardiology.
b: Coronary dominance: 85% right‑dominant (RCA supplies posterior descending artery).
Persistent left superior vena cava may be encountered during central line placement.
Bicuspid aortic valve (≈1% prevalence) predisposes to early stenosis.
Atrial septal defect (ostium secundum) often asymptomatic but can cause right‑sided volume overload.

sections.p: A systematic bedside assessment integrates anatomy with physiology to generate a focused differential.
b: Inspect: chest wall deformities, scars, visible pulsations.
Palpate: apex beat location, heave, thrills, peripheral pulses.
Auscultate: heart sounds in the four standard positions (aortic, pulmonic, tricuspid, mitral).
Assess JVP: height above the sternal angle reflects right atrial pressure.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain with diaphoresis or syncope
New onset severe dyspnoea with orthopnoea
Rapidly rising JVP with muffled heart sounds (possible tamponade)

faq.q: Why is the apex beat used to estimate left ventricular size?
faq.a: The left ventricle forms the apex; enlargement pushes the point laterally and inferiorly, making it palpable outside the normal 5th intercostal space.

faq.q: What does a displaced point of maximal impulse indicate?
faq.a: A laterally displaced PMI suggests left ventricular dilation or hypertrophy, common in chronic hypertension or valvular disease.

faq.q: How can I differentiate a pericardial friction rub from a pleural rub?
faq.a: A pericardial rub is heard best with the patient leaning forward, varies with respiration, and is heard over the left lower sternal border; a pleural rub follows the respiratory cycle and is louder at the lung bases.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a laterally displaced apex beat and a systolic murmur at the apex – what is the most likely anatomic lesion and why? — Likely mitral regurgitation; displaced apex reflects LV enlargement, holosystolic murmur radiates to axilla.

During a trauma survey you find a new left‑sided sternal tenderness and a paradoxical pulse – which cardiac structure is most likely injured and what immediate step is required? — Possible right ventricular contusion; monitor for arrhythmia and obtain bedside echocardiography.

A patient with known rheumatic fever develops a diastolic murmur best heard at the apex – which valve is affected and what anatomical change produces the murmur? — Mitral stenosis; thickened leaflets and reduced orifice cause turbulent flow during diastole.

Explain how coronary artery dominance influences the area of infarction in an LAD occlusion – which myocardial region is jeopardised? — In left‑dominant hearts the LAD supplies a larger portion of the posterior wall; occlusion leads to extensive anterior‑posterior infarction.

You have only a stethoscope and a sphygmomanometer; how would you assess for possible cardiac tamponade? — Look for Beck’s triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVP elevation) and assess pulsus paradoxus by measuring BP during inspiration.

A newborn is found to have a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border; what congenital anomaly should you suspect and what anatomic feature explains it? — Ventricular septal defect; left‑to‑right shunt across the interventricular septum creates turbulence.

Why is the right coronary artery more commonly the dominant vessel, and how does this affect surgical planning for aortic valve replacement? — RCA supplies the posterior descending artery in most people; dominance determines which coronary ostium must be protected during cross‑clamping.

A patient with hypertension shows a sustained left ventricular heave; which anatomical change does this reflect and what is its clinical significance? — Concentric LV hypertrophy; indicates pressure overload and predicts future heart failure.

How does the Frank‑Starling mechanism relate to the physical finding of a ‘full’ versus ‘empty’ jugular venous pulse? — Increased preload stretches myocardial fibers, enhancing stroke volume; a ‘full’ JVP reflects high preload, while an ‘empty’ JVP suggests low preload.

In a low‑resource setting without echocardiography, what combination of bedside signs can reliably suggest severe aortic stenosis? — Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, weak delayed carotid upstroke, and a narrow pulse pressure.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Collect key symptoms, then perform a focused cardiac exam. A clear history guides which signs to look for and what a positive finding implies.
b: History: • Chest pain (character, radiation, triggers) • Dyspnoea (on exertion, orthopnoea) • Palpitations (irregularity, frequency) • Swelling (legs, abdomen) • Syncope or near‑syncope episodes
History: • Past cardiac disease, rheumatic fever, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, family history
Examination: • Inspection – jugular venous distension, peripheral oedema, cyanosis
Examination: • Palpation – apex beat location, heave, thrill, displaced point of maximal impulse
Examination: • Percussion – cardiac dullness, displaced heart border
Examination: • Auscultation – S1/S2 quality, murmurs (location, timing, radiation), gallops (S3/S4), rubs
Examination: • Special tests – Korotkoff phases for blood pressure, hand‑grip test for LV hypertrophy
Bedside test limits – cannot quantify ejection fraction, cannot detect silent ischemia, cannot differentiate valve pathology without imaging

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a structured table to match each test with its clinical question, interpretation, and action when unavailable.

t.b: Detects arrhythmias, ischemia, infarction, conduction blocks; look for ST‑segment changes, Q waves, T‑wave inversion, axis deviation. If unavailable, use handheld ECG or pulse oximetry for rhythm assessment.
Assesses cardiac size, pulmonary congestion, pleural effusion. Cardiomegaly > 50% of thoracic width suggests LV hypertrophy or failure. If not available, use bedside ultrasound for size.
Measures EF, valve morphology, wall thickness, pericardial effusion. EF < 40% = HFrEF. If TTE unavailable, use point‑of‑care ultrasound or Doppler.
Biomarker for heart failure; > 400 pg/mL (age‑adjusted) indicates decompensation. If assay unavailable, rely on clinical signs and imaging.
Defines coronary anatomy, occlusion sites, dominance. If not available, use CT coronary angiography or fractional flow reserve.
Gold standard for fibrosis, viability, RV function. If unavailable, use TTE with contrast.
Detects paroxysmal arrhythmias; > 30 premature beats/min suggests atrial fibrillation risk. If not available, use event recorder or bedside ECG.
Identifies anemia, electrolyte imbalance, renal dysfunction affecting cardiac function. If unavailable, use clinical assessment of hydration and perfusion.

sections.p: A systematic approach ensures timely treatment, safe monitoring and appropriate escalation for cardiac conditions in low‑resource settings.
b: Initial assessment: ABCs, oxygen, rapid bedside ECG, and focused history to identify life‑threatening arrhythmia or ischemia.
First‑line pharmacology: beta‑blocker (e.g., propranolol) for tachyarrhythmia, ACE inhibitor for heart failure, and diuretic (furosemide) for volume overload; avoid NSAIDs in heart failure.
Definitive therapy: reperfusion (thrombolysis if PCI unavailable), valve surgery for severe regurgitation, or device implantation for refractory arrhythmia.
Monitoring: repeat ECG, vitals every 15 min initially, urine output, and daily weight; watch for signs of decompensation.
Escalation criteria: persistent hypotension, worsening chest pain, new pulmonary edema, or arrhythmia unresponsive to drugs – refer for higher‑level care.
Discharge planning: education on medication adherence, lifestyle, and follow‑up schedule; arrange community health worker visits if possible.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding adverse reactions and interactions helps prevent iatrogenic harm, especially where laboratory monitoring is limited.
b: Beta‑blockers may cause bradycardia and bronchospasm – stop if heart rate <50 bpm or wheeze develops; consider cardioselective agent.
ACE inhibitors can precipitate renal impairment – check creatinine if possible; hold drug if rise >30 % or potassium >5.5 mmol/L.
Loop diuretics cause electrolyte loss – supplement potassium orally if serum K⁺ falls below 3.5 mmol/L; monitor for dehydration.
Aspirin increases bleeding risk – avoid in active gastrointestinal ulcer or severe thrombocytopenia; use proton‑pump inhibitor if ulcer risk high.
Digoxin toxicity presents with nausea, visual halos, and arrhythmia – stop drug and give activated charcoal if recent ingestion; monitor serum level when feasible.
Thrombolytics may cause intracranial hemorrhage – contraindicated in recent head trauma or uncontrolled hypertension; observe for severe headache or neurological change.

sections.p: Prompt recognition of complications guides timely referral to tertiary centres.
b: Cardiogenic shock: systolic BP <90 mmHg, cool extremities, oliguria – start inotropes, consider intra‑aortic balloon pump, refer urgently.
Acute pulmonary edema: severe dyspnea, crackles, pink frothy sputum – give high‑flow oxygen, IV furosemide, and consider non‑invasive ventilation; transfer if no improvement.
Ventricular arrhythmia (VT/VF): loss of pulse or unstable rhythm – immediate defibrillation, amiodarone infusion, and rapid transfer.
Pericardial tamponade: muffled heart sounds, JVD, hypotension (Beck's triad) – perform emergency pericardiocentesis; arrange surgical drainage.
Stroke secondary to atrial fibrillation: new focal deficit – start anticoagulation if no contraindication, arrange neuro‑imaging and specialist input.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities modify presentation, investigations and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV infection: higher risk of myocarditis and pericardial effusion; avoid nephrotoxic drugs if on tenofovir; monitor for drug‑drug interactions with protease inhibitors.
Tuberculosis: pericardial TB can mimic effusion; obtain pericardial fluid for acid‑fast stain; treat with standard anti‑TB regimen before steroids.
Malnutrition: low albumin worsens drug binding and edema; use lower diuretic doses and monitor electrolytes closely.
Pregnancy: avoid ACE inhibitors and warfarin; use heparin for anticoagulation and beta‑blockers that are pregnancy‑safe.
Diabetes: beta‑blockers may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms; choose agents with less effect on glucose and monitor blood sugar.
Alcohol abuse: predisposes to dilated cardiomyopathy; counsel cessation and avoid binge‑drinking before surgery.
Renal failure: limit ACE inhibitor dose, avoid contrast‑enhanced imaging, and adjust diuretic regimen.
Liver disease: coagulopathy affects anticoagulation decisions; use low‑molecular‑weight heparin with careful monitoring.

sections.p: Tailoring care to vulnerable populations improves outcomes where resources are scarce.
b: Children: use weight‑based dosing, prefer echocardiography over CT, and consider congenital lesions first; avoid adult‑dose ACE inhibitors.
Pregnant women: prioritize non‑teratogenic drugs, use low‑dose aspirin for prophylaxis, and plan delivery in a centre with cardiac anaesthesia.
Elderly: start all drugs at half the usual dose, watch for orthostatic hypotension, and prefer once‑daily regimens for adherence.
People with HIV: screen for drug interactions with antiretrovirals, use echocardiography to detect early cardiomyopathy, and vaccinate against pneumococcus.
Low‑resource settings: rely on clinical scoring (e.g., Killip class), use streptokinase if PCI unavailable, and train community health workers for follow‑up.

facts: Apex beat normally located at the left 5th intercostal space, mid‑clavicular line.
Normal sinus rhythm: 60–100 bpm; bradycardia <60 bpm, tachycardia >100 bpm.
Coronary dominance: right dominant in ~85 % of people, left dominant ~8 %, balanced ~7 %.
Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate; normal 4.5–5.5 L/min.
S3 gallop indicates rapid ventricular filling; common in heart failure with EF < 40 %.
Mitral valve area <1.5 cm² defines severe mitral stenosis.
Aortic stenosis severity: peak velocity >4 m/s, mean gradient >40 mmHg, valve area <1.0 cm².
Jugular venous pressure >3 cm above sternal angle suggests elevated right atrial pressure.
Pericardial tamponade: pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg drop in systolic BP on inspiration.

vivas.q: What is the most common congenital heart defect causing a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border in a newborn?
vivas.a: Ventricular septal defect; a left‑to‑right shunt producing a harsh holosystolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border.

vivas.q: Which valve is most frequently involved in rheumatic heart disease?
vivas.a: The mitral valve, typically presenting with mitral regurgitation early and mitral stenosis later.

vivas.q: A 70‑year‑old heart‑transplant recipient has fever, pulmonary infiltrates and a KOH prep showing budding yeast. Which antifungal mechanism is first‑line?
vivas.a: Inhibition of fungal cell membrane ergosterol synthesis (e.g., azole class).

vivas.q: What does the presence of oval budding yeast with pseudohyphae on KOH indicate in a transplant patient?
vivas.a: Candida species infection; suggests invasive candidiasis requiring systemic antifungal therapy.

vivas.q: A drug blocks muscarinic receptors in the heart. What is the expected effect on heart rate?
vivas.a: Increase in heart rate (tachycardia) because vagal slowing is removed.

vivas.q: Which behavioural intervention is most appropriate for a patient with health anxiety repeatedly seeking reassurance for cardiac symptoms?
vivas.a: Cognitive‑behavioural therapy focusing on health anxiety and reassurance avoidance.

vivas.q: During a public presentation, a student experiences rapid heart rate and dry mouth. Which autonomic division mediates these signs?
vivas.a: Sympathetic division – releases norepinephrine causing tachycardia and reduces salivation.

vivas.q: What is the primary molecular mechanism of doxorubicin‑induced cardiotoxicity?
vivas.a: Generation of free radicals causing oxidative damage to myocardial cell membranes and mitochondrial DNA.

vivas.q: In chronic heart failure with EF 30 %, what compensatory mechanism worsens pulmonary congestion?
vivas.a: Activation of the renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system leading to sodium and water retention and increased preload.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate a pericardial friction rub from a pleural rub on auscultation?
vivas.a: Pericardial rub is heard best with the patient leaning forward, has three components (two systolic, one diastolic), and does not vary with respiration; pleural rub varies with breathing.

vivas.q: Why is a high‑flow oxygen mask avoided in a patient with known COPD exacerbation and CO₂ retention?
vivas.a: Excessive oxygen can suppress hypoxic drive, worsening hypercapnia.

vivas.q: What clinical sign indicates cardiac tamponade on blood pressure measurement?
vivas.a: Pulsus paradoxus – >10 mmHg drop in systolic pressure during inspiration.

vivas.q: Explain how right coronary artery dominance influences the area of infarction in an LAD occlusion.
vivas.a: In right‑dominant hearts, the posterior descending artery arises from the RCA; LAD occlusion spares the inferior wall, which is supplied by the RCA.

vivas.q: What is the bedside maneuver to assess for a left‑sided sternal fracture after trauma?
vivas.a: Palpate the sternum for step deformity and crepitus; ask the patient to cough and note localized tenderness.

vivas.q: How would you assess for cardiac tamponade using only a stethoscope and sphygmomanometer?
vivas.a: Listen for muffled heart sounds and measure for pulsus paradoxus; a >10 mmHg inspiratory drop suggests tamponade.

vivas.q: What is the significance of a laterally displaced apex beat with a systolic murmur at the apex?
vivas.a: Suggests left ventricular enlargement (e.g., dilated cardiomyopathy) with mitral regurgitation.

vivas.q: Why is the left coronary artery less often dominant?
vivas.a: Embryologically, the right coronary artery persists as the primary source for the posterior descending artery in most individuals.

vivas.q: What is the key difference between atrial septal defect and patent foramen ovale on echocardiography?
vivas.a: ASD shows a true anatomical opening with left‑to‑right shunt; PFO is a flap‑like opening that may only open with transient right‑to‑left pressure reversal.

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old man presents with exertional dyspnoea, a harsh systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, and a thrill. Which lesion is most likely?
mcqs.e: VSD produces a harsh holosystolic murmur with a palpable thrill at the left lower sternal border.

mcqs.q: Which ECG finding is most specific for acute pericarditis?
o: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression
Q waves in leads II, III, aVF
mcqs.e: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression is classic for pericarditis.

mcqs.q: A patient with right‑dominant coronary anatomy suffers an inferior myocardial infarction. Which artery is occluded?
mcqs.e: In right‑dominant hearts the RCA gives rise to the posterior descending artery supplying the inferior wall.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a contraindication to beta‑blocker use in acute decompensated heart failure?
o: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
mcqs.e: Severe bradycardia can be worsened by beta‑blockers and is a contraindication.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource setting, which bedside test best estimates left ventricular systolic function?
mcqs.e: A sustained, displaced apex beat suggests left ventricular hypertrophy or dilatation, hinting at reduced function.

mcqs.q: Which sign distinguishes cardiac from hepatic ascites on physical exam?
mcqs.e: Positive hepato‑jugular reflux indicates elevated right‑sided pressures, favouring cardiac ascites.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with sudden onset chest pain radiating to the back, hypotension (BP 90/60 mmHg), muffled heart sounds and jugular venous distension.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.a: Cardiac tamponade, likely due to aortic dissection rupture into the pericardium.

qs.q: Which bedside maneuver confirms the diagnosis with limited equipment?
qs.a: Measure pulsus paradoxus with a sphygmomanometer; a drop >10 mmHg on inspiration supports tamponade.

qs.q: What is the immediate management step?
qs.a: Urgent pericardiocentesis under echocardiographic guidance, followed by surgical repair of the underlying cause.

cases.v: A 3‑month‑old infant is brought for a routine check‑up. On auscultation a grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border. The infant is thriving, with no cyanosis.

qs.q: What is the most probable cardiac lesion?
qs.a: Small ventricular septal defect (VSD) with left‑to‑right shunt.

qs.q: What investigation would you order to confirm the diagnosis?
qs.a: Echocardiography with colour Doppler to visualise the defect and assess shunt size.

qs.q: What is the typical management for a small VSD in this age group?
qs.a: Observation and regular follow‑up; most small VSDs close spontaneously without intervention.

mistakes: Confusing a VSD murmur (holosystolic) with a mitral regurgitation murmur (also holosystolic but best heard at the apex).
Assuming all patients with tamponade have pulsus paradoxus; it may be absent in early stages.
Using the term ‘right‑dominant’ to imply better prognosis; dominance only affects infarct distribution.
Prescribing beta‑blockers in acute decompensated heart failure without checking for severe bradycardia or hypotension.
Over‑relying on chest X‑ray for diagnosing pericardial effusion; bedside ultrasound is far more sensitive.
Mistaking a pericardial friction rub for a pleural rub by not noting its independence from respiration.
Failing to differentiate a patent foramen ovale from an atrial septal defect on echo, leading to inappropriate closure decisions.
Neglecting to assess for pulsus paradoxus when only a stethoscope and sphygmomanometer are available.
